intro: Currently, all these medications are **approved by the FDA** (U.S. Food and Drug Administration) exclusively **for treating specific diseases** – diabetes, obesity, or for suppressing the immune system after organ transplantation. Any use of them by healthy people for so-called “rejuvenation” is strictly off-label and carries significant risks.
highlights: None of these therapies have proven to extend human lifespan.
GLP-1 drugs may support healthy aging through weight loss and metabolic benefits.
Metformin shows potential, but human longevity evidence remains limited.
Rapamycin improves some aging markers, yet no rejuvenation has been proven.
Sleep, exercise, and nutrition remain the most effective longevity tools.

blocks.text: Semaglutide and GLP-1: More Than Just a Weight Loss Shot

You may have heard of Ozempic or Wegovy – these are the commercial names for GLP-1 class drugs. Originally, they were created for people with type 2 diabetes to help the pancreas produce insulin. Later, it turned out that patients on these drugs rapidly lose weight because the medication signals the brain: “I’m full.”

But why did aging researchers suddenly become interested in them? The answer lies in their profound impact on the cardiovascular system and their ability to reduce systemic inflammation, which is one of the main drivers of the body’s aging process.

What Did Animal Studies Show?

An [article](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-10940-7) published in the journal Nature describes an experiment on laboratory mice aged 20 months – from a biological standpoint, this is the equivalent of deep old age in humans.

When rodents were given semaglutide, their bodies started acting as if the animals were on a strict, [healthy diet](https://www.biohackers.world/blog/biohacking-diet). In biology, it is known that significant calorie restriction (when the body is underfed but gets all its vitamins) is the only reliable way to extend the life of animals. The drug was able to mimic this effect without actual starvation.
**What changed inside the mice?**

items: **Neurogenesis:** The drug stimulated the formation of new neurons in the hippocampus (the memory center), which practically translated into a significant improvement in the animals’ cognitive functions.
**Rejuvenating hematopoiesis:** The number of pro-inflammatory blood stem cells decreased. The levels of cellular aging markers (such as p16, p21) and systemic inflammation dropped sharply.

**Energy metabolism:** There was an increase in [NAD+ levels](https://www.biohackers.world/blog/the-science-of-nad-benefits-risks) (a molecule critically important for cellular energy) and enhanced activity of aging-regulating proteins.

blocks.text: The Debate on Real Impact: Does it work the same way in humans?
This is where the most interesting part begins in the scientific world – a real debate.

items: **Optimists** (aging researchers) point to the direct molecular impact of GLP-1 receptors on brain and vascular tissues, arguing that the drug has an**independent rejuvenating effect.**
**Skeptics** (clinicians and endocrinologists) note that almost all positive changes in the human body can be explained as a **secondary effect of weight loss.**

blocks.text: When a person loses dangerous fat around their internal organs (visceral fat), their blood pressure automatically drops, and kidney and heart functions improve. The body simply stops working at the absolute limit of its capabilities.

**What healthy people need to remember:** For a completely healthy person **without excess weight** , these drugs may **not be an anti-aging preventative** – if clinicians are right in their skepticism. Furthermore, they have unpleasant side effects: nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. And most importantly – we still don’t know how these drugs will affect a healthy person’s body if they take them for 10 or 20 years.
Metformin: A Cheap Pill with a Hundreds-of-Years-Old History

If GLP-1 is an expensive and trendy novelty, metformin is a good old friend. Doctors have been prescribing this oral medication (pill) to diabetics for over 60 years. Its origins are linked to the extract of the French lilac (Galega officinalis), which was used in medicine as far back as the 17th century.
The Paradox That Caught Scientists’ Attention

A few years ago, scientists analyzed the medical records of thousands of people and noticed a strange paradox. Patients with diabetes who took metformin daily lived longer and had fewer heart or oncology problems than… absolutely healthy people without diabetes. This caused a real shock in the medical community.
Mimicking Energy Deficit
The mechanism of action can be compared to an **energy-saving mode** in complex systems. In the cell, the AMPK enzyme acts as the main energy sensor.

items: Metformin can partially inhibit the work of mitochondria (cellular powerhouses).
This lowers energy levels (ATP) and simultaneously reduces the release of harmful free radicals.

This activates the AMPK enzyme, which shifts the cell into a state of “physiological deficit.” The cell stops actively dividing and begins to use resources economically, while simultaneously repairing damaged structures.

blocks.text: Animal studies have shown **mixed results** . In laboratory conditions, this mechanism extended the lifespan of nematodes (Caenorhabditis elegans) by almost 50%. But when it was given to fruit flies or rats, they **didn’t live a single day longer.**

Why should healthy people be careful?

Currently, a massive study called TAME (Targeting Aging with Metformin) is being prepared in the US. Scientists want to test whether metformin can really delay the onset of age-related diseases in older adults.
But while there are no results yet, many healthy young people have already started taking it “just in case.” And here lies the danger:

items: **It can “steal” your workout results.** When you exercise, your body experiences stress and gets stronger, so it will be easier next time. Metformin partially blocks this process – studies indicate that the drug can suppress positive mitochondrial adaptation in muscles in response to aerobic training.
**Vitamin deficiency.** Long-term use can lead to a severe lack of vitamin B12 in the blood.

**Genetic compatibility.** Due to the specifics of the microbiome (gut bacteria) and certain genes (specifically, the OCT1 gene), metformin might be **beneficial for one person** and **completely useless for another.**

blocks.text: Rapamycin and the Concept of Rapamycin Longevity: A Powerful but Dangerous Tool
The story of rapamycin began in the 1970s with the discovery of an unknown bacterium in soil samples from Easter Island (Rapa Nui).

Later, it turned out that this substance – rapamycin – can powerfully suppress the immune system. It began to be used in medicine so that a patient’s body wouldn’t reject a new kidney or heart after a transplant. But today, the term rapamycin longevityhas become a major trend in aging research.
Regulation of Cell Growth and Triggering Autophagy

The main target of the drug is the **mTOR protein complex** . This is a kind of master dispatcher in every one of our cells. When there is plenty of food, mTOR presses the “gas pedal” – stimulates active protein synthesis and tissue growth.

But with age, this pedal often gets stuck. The body is no longer growing, but mTOR activity often remains pathologically high. This leads to mistakes: the formation of cancerous tumors or the accumulation of cellular garbage, which provokes Alzheimer’s disease.
Rapamycin strictly blocks this pathway. It tells the cell: “There are no resources, stop” – forcing it to switch to a **preservation mode.**
This triggers **autophagy** – a vital process during which the cell destroys and recycles damaged proteins and organelles, clearing tissues of toxic ballast.
For laboratory mice, this worked phenomenally. The mechanism provided a stable lifespan extension **of 9–14%.**

Until recently, translating these successes to humans remained purely theoretical. However, the situation was changed by the [PEARL study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40188830/) (results published in the spring of 2025) – the longest randomized, placebo-controlled trial of rapamycin in healthy older adults to date.
PEARL Study Results
Over 48 weeks, participants took low, intermittent doses of the drug (5 mg or 10 mg once a week). The results proved highly revealing, debunking both certain myths and the biggest fears:

items: **The main disappointment:** Rapamycin did not affect whatsoever on the amount of visceral fat (the internal fat surrounding the organs). Additionally, DNA methylation analysis showed that the participants’ epigenetic age did not change – meaning **no actual ‘rejuvenation’ occurred at the cellular level.**

**Unexpected specific wins:** Women taking the 10 mg dose showed a statistically significant increase in lean muscle mass and a noticeable reduction in pain symptoms (according to the WOMAC questionnaire).

**Subjective improvement:** The group taking 5 mg reported a significant improvement in their emotional state and overall sense of health, although this was not backed by drastic changes in blood tests.”

blocks.text: **Side Effects**

Despite concerns about severe immunosuppression, clinical data from the PEARL study paint a more optimistic picture regarding the safety of specifically low, intermittent doses (5-10 mg once a week). Over 48 weeks, the rate of serious side effects in the rapamycin group was roughly the same as in the placebo group.
If you don’t turn the protocol into **extreme ‘biohacking,’** low-dose therapy is well tolerated by healthy adults.
**The problem of bioavailability and standardization**
Longevity clinics often use ‘compounded’ (custom-made in a pharmacy setting) rapamycin instead of expensive commercial drugs.

However, during the PEARL study, it turned out that such capsules have critically low absorption: the drug concentration in patients’ blood was only **about 33%** compared to standardized commercial formulas.
Expectations vs. Reality

rows: Myth you might hear online
Scientific reality
These drugs have already been proven to extend human life.
No pharmacological agent today has clinical proof of extending the maximum human lifespan.
Rapamycin is a safe anti-aging supplement.
It is a serious prescription immunosuppressant with proven risks of infections and metabolic disorders.
GLP-1 (Ozempic) was created specifically to fight aging.
It is a medication for diabetes and weight control; its longevity benefits may come primarily as a consequence of cardiometabolic improvement.
Metformin should be taken by all healthy people for prevention.
The drug can block positive muscle adaptation to exercise and has varying effectiveness depending on individual genetics.

blocks.text: What to Do About Aging Today?
The study of GLP-1 drugs, metformin, and the deep dive into the concept of rapamycin longevity are opening a new era in the understanding of cellular biology.

But today, the use of these serious prescription drugs by absolutely healthy people remains a medical experiment with no safety guarantees. The body is a complex ecosystem. Trying to “fix” one thing (artificially turning on cellular cleanup) can easily break another (the immune system).
While scientists spend years conducting clinical trials to find safe doses, the most effective longevity strategy remains what always works:

items: **Quality sleep** (this is the best time for that very autophagy and brain cleanup).
**Strength and cardio training** (natural stimulation of mitochondria).
**A balanced diet** without an excess of processed foods.

blocks.text: The pharmacology of the future will definitely give us new tools, but for now, the best medicine for old age requires discipline from us, not a prescription from the pharmacy.
